title: Smartphone and application-store ecosystem from integrated device to programmable mobile platform
pressure: Mobile phones, portable media and internet access existed as partially separate experiences; useful third-party mobile software also faced distribution and device-fragmentation friction.
preExistingWorldModel: Feature phones, PDAs, mobile browsers, carrier portals and desktop software distribution were mature but did not form one dominant touch-centric programmable consumer platform.
candidateRoutes: SDK plus centrally operated application store
open-source mobile operating system plus user-driven application market
observationsAndInstruments: Apple introduced iPhone in 2007 as an integrated phone, media and internet device with a multi-touch interface.
Apple exposed a native SDK and launched the App Store in 2008; application supply and downloads grew immediately.
Android released source code and launched Android Market with the first Android phone in October 2008, using materially different governance/distribution choices.
decisiveTests: can one mobile hardware/software system make web/media/phone interaction usable at scale
can external developers ship native applications to users with low distribution friction
can different platform-governance models attract durable complements
technicalOrScientificTransition: The mobile device became a programmable ecosystem in which hardware, OS, SDK, identity/payment, distribution, review/governance, radio networks and third-party applications jointly produced capability.
rivalsAndFailures: Apple and Android used different openness and application-admission models.
A strong integrated device alone did not generate the later application ecosystem without developer and distribution infrastructure.
diffusionAndScaling: Application marketplaces and additional devices/carriers expanded the platform beyond the initial handset.
standardsAndInstitutions: Platform owners, carriers, developers, application stores and standards bodies controlled different interfaces and admission points.
externalitiesAndCorrections: Centralized application distribution reduced some friction while also concentrating platform governance and admission power.
secondOrderEffects: The platform shifted innovation outward toward millions of third-party software producers and created new mobile service/business categories.
sourceNativeSummary: The smartphone transition was a system integration plus ecosystem-construction trajectory, not merely a better handset: device, SDK, store/market, network and governance choices co-produced the capability.
